.@JDRF advocates have made huge progress for Americans living with diabetes

Today, the Senate Health Committee successfully advanced my bill w/ @SenatorShaheen to support & strengthen the Special Diabetes Program – our most strategic effort to combat diabetes & its complications

Our country continues to face a growing doctor shortage crisis, particularly in our rural areas.

That’s why we introduced this bipartisan bill to support the training opportunities that are needed to bridge this gap & improve access to health care. 

https://t.co/5l3bbaqerm

Right now, far too many Americans are forced to ration life-saving medicine — like the 8.4 million that rely on insulin.
 
That’s why @SenatorShaheen and I are leading the way to dramatically reduce the cost of this lifesaving drug.  Read more here: https://t.co/NbnIOVuKMo

Visiting Eastern Maine Community College in Bangor today, I had the chance to see how investments in new classroom technology and training equipment are helping to ensure that graduates are well prepared to enter the health care workforce. I was proud to secure nearly $3 million in Congressionally Directed Spending to support EMCC’s efforts to train Maine’s next generation of nurses, emergency medical service providers, medical radiographers, and other health professionals to help confront our state and nation’s shortage of workers in this important field.

At an Appropriations hearing to review the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) budget, I pressed the NIH Director on the Administration’s proposal to cut funding for biomedical research. These cuts would result in a nearly 40% reduction in funding for the National Institute on Aging, which supports most Alzheimer’s research.

As progress is finally being made with early detection tools and treatments that can slow Alzheimer’s disease, now is not the time to slash funding. Through my role as Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I will continue to fight for funding to support lifesaving biomedical research.

I strongly support extending the tax relief for families and small businesses. My vote against this bill stems primarily from the harmful impact it will have on Medicaid, affecting low-income families and rural health care providers like our hospitals and nursing homes.

The Medicaid program has been an important health care safety net for nearly 60 years that has helped people in difficult financial circumstances, including people with disabilities, children, seniors, and low-income families. Approximately 400,000 Mainers – nearly a third of the state's population – depend on this program.

This week, Senator Tina Smith and I introduced a bill to reauthorize our Kay Hagan Tick Act so that we can continue to support important research, diagnostics, prevention, and treatment of tick-borne diseases by providing targeted funding for state health departments and regional Centers of Excellence.

Earlier this year, I spoke at the Center for Lyme Action Congressional Series about the progress we have made thanks to Kay Hagan Tick Act, including the first-ever clinical trial for a Lyme disease vaccine for humans, which is underway right now at the MaineHealth Institute for Research. With Lyme disease cases hitting a record high of more than 3,000 last year in the State of Maine, this reauthorization is urgently needed.

The Senate Health Committee today unanimously advanced my bipartisan bill to reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, which I first authored in 2019 with Senator Tina Smith. This legislation would continue our ongoing federal response to Lyme and other tick-borne diseases, and honors our late colleague Senator Kay Hagan, who tragically passed away from complications of the Powassan virus, a rare but serious tick-borne illness.

Maine reported a record 3,218 cases of Lyme disease last year—more than double the number from just five years ago. With cases of tick-borne illnesses increasing at such an alarming rate, reauthorizing this law is critical to continuing our ongoing research, prevention, and public health efforts. I now look forward to working with my colleagues to pass this reauthorization on the Senate floor.

Our nation is facing a severe shortage of geriatric health professionals and direct service workers while the number of older Americans continues to rise rapidly. That is why, this week, I introduced the bipartisan Geriatrics Workforce Improvement Act with Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia to reauthorize the only federally funded programs specifically designed to develop a health care workforce focused on the care of older Americans.

This bill would invest nearly $50 million per year over the next five years to fund the training of more geriatric care providers and strengthen support for family caregivers. With Maine having the oldest population in the nation, this investment is especially critical for our state.

It was a great honor to be invited to speak at the World Medical Innovation Forum this week and hear firsthand from so many experts driving innovation and patient care. 

From strengthening our health agencies and supporting rural hospitals, to ensuring access to Medicaid and advancing medical breakthroughs, our work must focus on protecting patients, empowering researchers, and maintaining America’s global leadership in health and science.

Rural hospitals and community health providers rely on the 340B drug pricing program to keep care affordable and accessible for patients in need. These savings allow providers to reduce prescription costs, expand services, and care for more Mainers. As we consider changes to the 340B program, we must preserve the flexibility that allows providers to use these savings to meet local needs, especially at a time when so many of our rural health providers are struggling.

At a Health Committee hearing today, I shared how Hometown Health Center in Newport uses 340B savings to cover medications for patients facing financial hardship and to provide transportation for homebound patients. These services make a real difference in people’s lives, and we risk losing them if changes to the program reduce critical funding rural providers need.

In the time since, the people of Lewiston have shown remarkable resilience and unity. We recognize the law enforcement officers, medical professionals, and neighbors who rushed to help, and we stand with the city as it continues to rebuild and heal. Their courage and compassion reflect the very best of Maine, and their example continues to inspire us all.

I am pleased that this approval will allow our state to make historic investments in expanding its high-speed network and will ensure that thousands more Mainers have a reliable connection to their loved ones, co-workers, schools, and medical services.

I was honored to receive the Legislator of the Year Award from the @amerambassoc, which represents many of the dedicated men and women who respond to medical emergencies every day.
 
To support these providers and their lifesaving work, this past year, I introduced the bipartisan Protecting Access to Ground Ambulance Medical Services Act to extend and increase Medicare add-on payments for EMS agencies. I also partnered with Senator Welch of Vermont on the Comprehensive Alternative Response to Emergencies (CARE) Act, which would create a Medicare pilot model to reimburse EMS providers for treatment in place, not just transport, saving patients money and ensuring fair compensation for care provided by EMS professionals.
 
I will continue working to ensure that EMS providers have the resources they need to care for patients and save lives, regardless of someone’s ZIP code.

Alzheimer’s is one of the greatest public health challenges of our time, affecting more than seven million Americans, including nearly 29,000 people in Maine. Early diagnosis is essential, yet too many patients continue to go undiagnosed until their symptoms become severe.

That is why, today, I introduced bipartisan legislation that would require the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to create a pathway to cover blood biomarker tests approved by the FDA for the early detection of Alzheimer’s disease. The FDA approved the first blood-based biomarker test for use by primary care physicians earlier this year, but physicians could be hesitant to use the tests if they are not reimbursed by CMS.

The Alzheimer’s Screening and Prevention Act would expand access to earlier testing, giving patients and their families more time to plan, seek support, and pursue the best options for care for their loved ones.

Thank you to the @alzassociation for endorsing this legislation and for their tireless advocacy on behalf of Americans living with this disease. Earlier this year, I joined their annual Alzheimer’s Impact Movement Advocacy Forum in Washington to recognize the Association’s efforts to ensure that Alzheimer’s remains a national priority.

It was wonderful to visit Northern Light AR Gould Hospital today to meet with staff members and see their new Linear Accelerator radiation therapy equipment for cancer patients. The hardworking health care professionals at AR Gould provide critical and compassionate care for their patients, and I am delighted to have been able to join them in celebrating this great advancement in cancer care for Mainers in The County.
 
I am proud to have secured $3.016 million in federal funding as Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee to support the purchase of this machine, which will provide patients across northern Maine access to cutting-edge cancer treatment and innovative health care solutions.

It is great news that funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program has been released by the Department of Health and Human Services, with nearly $40 million going to the State of Maine and five Maine Tribal governments.

Last month, @SenJackReed, @lisamurkowski, and I wrote DHHS urging the prompt release of funding for the program, which will help low-income households and seniors on fixed incomes in Maine afford their energy bills this winter.

LIHEAP funds help Mainers avoid the constant worry of having to choose between heating their homes and covering other basic necessities. As Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I will continue to support this program and work to better ensure that households in Maine and throughout the country can afford to keep their homes warm and safe throughout the winter.

It is wonderful news that the Department of Health and Human Services has announced its decision to add Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) to the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel for newborn children, following a written request from me and a bipartisan group of nine congressional colleagues.

Throughout my Senate service, supporting research and early detection for Duchenne muscular dystrophy and other rare diseases has been one of my highest priorities. DMD is often not diagnosed until patients are four or five years old, when meaningful muscle loss has already occurred. This decision from HHS will allow families to get answers at birth and take advantage of the growing list of FDA-approved therapies at a time when they can make the greatest difference in slowing the progression of this devastating disease.

Great news today for Maine’s rural hospitals and health care providers as the state has been awarded $190 million through the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) in the first of five funding cycles. I proposed the $50 billion RHTP initiative—the largest single federal investment in rural health care in more than two decades—earlier this year to help give rural states like Maine the resources they need to keep health care available close to home.

This funding will strengthen rural hospitals and support innovative approaches to lower costs and improve health outcomes for Mainers, no matter where they live. And while this investment will not solve every challenge facing our state’s rural health care system, it will improve access to care for individuals across rural Maine at a time when many rural health care providers are facing significant financial hardship.

Maine’s population is the oldest of any state in the nation and is among the most rural, making continued support for rural health care providers critical to ensuring that more Mainers can receive timely medical care when they need it.
